title: Streaming APIs and large payloads
description: Serve CSV exports, large files, and live data feeds without running out of memory. Learn chunked responses, `IAsyncEnumerable`, push-based streaming, and when to avoid buffering.

data.text: A naive API loads every row into memory, serializes the entire payload, and returns it in one giant response. For 10,000 rows that might be fine. For 10 million rows or a continuously updating feed, that approach crashes the server with an out-of-memory exception and makes clients wait minutes before receiving the first byte.
Streaming sends data in chunks as it is produced. The client starts processing immediately, the server never holds the full payload in memory, and both stay responsive regardless of dataset size.

items: Exports: CSV, Excel, JSONL, or NDJSON exports that can grow arbitrarily large.
Log and event feeds: tailing logs or event streams where data arrives continuously.
File downloads: serving large files without loading them fully into memory.
Real-time dashboards: pushing rows as they are generated instead of buffering a complete result.

data.text: If the total payload fits comfortably in memory and the client needs random access to the whole object, buffering is simpler and fine. Stream when the size is unbounded or the latency to first byte matters.

ASP.NET Core natively serializes `IAsyncEnumerable<T>` as a chunked JSON array. Each element is written to the response stream as it becomes available. The framework handles the response headers and the final closing bracket automatically.

data.title: Streaming orders as JSON

data.text: The client receives a standard JSON array but the server never materializes all rows at once. EF Core translates `AsAsyncEnumerable()` into a forward-only data reader that streams rows from SQL Server one at a time.

JSON arrays are convenient but require the client to parse a never-closing stream. For large exports, consider newline-delimited JSON (NDJSON) where each line is a complete JSON object. The client can process each line independently and stop parsing at any point.

data.title: Streaming NDJSON

data.text: For file downloads, use `PhysicalFileResult` or `PushStreamContent` to stream bytes directly from disk or from a generated PDF, Excel, or ZIP stream. Never read the entire file into a byte array unless the file is guaranteed to be small.

data.title: Streaming a large file

items: Do not call `.ToList()` or `.ToArray()` on a large query before yielding—this buffers everything.
Disable response buffering middleware if you have added it for other routes.
Avoid JSON serializers that buffer the full object graph; use the built-in System.Text.Json source-generated context for streaming.
Set `Response.Headers.TransferEncodingChunked = true` when the content length is unknown.

data.title: Monitoring tip
data.text: Streaming reduces memory but increases request duration. Monitor p99 latency and active connection count; a slow stream can exhaust the thread pool if clients read slowly.

data.title: Key takeaways
items: Use `IAsyncEnumerable` with EF Core to stream query results without loading them into memory.
Prefer NDJSON for large exports so clients can process records incrementally.
Pass the cancellation token through every async stream so cancelled requests stop work promptly.
Monitor streaming endpoints separately: they trade memory for duration and connection count.
